title: Treat AI Like a Normal Crisis
summary: One 27-year-old quit his job, and everybody (including but not limited to the singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow) appears to have lost it.The past two weeks have been dizzying. The 27-year-old, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, went public with an alarming allegation: That the people inside ...
content:
One 27-year-old quit his job, and everybody (including but not limited to the singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow) appears to have lost it.

The past two weeks have been dizzying. The 27-year-old, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, went public with an alarming allegation: That the people inside Silicon Valley’s leading AI companies truly believe their products might pose an extinction level threat to humanity. This claim isn’t exactly new. AI safety advocates, often dubbed doomers, have been saying this for over a decade. Coxon isn’t even the first AI researcher this year to quit and cite concerns.

Yet Coxon’s post went obscenely viral. It has been viewed more than 170 million times on X—orders of magnitude more than the usual, wonky discussions of “misaligned” or runaway AIs. If you’re reading this, you’ve likely seen some version of a headline that asks Is AI Really Going To Kill Us All? The debate isn’t just online. It has roiled Washington D.C., activating figures as disparate as Donald Trump and Barack Obama. Inside AI companies, researchers echoed Coxon’s concerns, and the heads of every major AI company publicly expressed the need to “pace the frontier,” another way of saying that they ought to slow future development. In recent days, it has come to seem as if the media, Silicon Valley, and the entire internet are all trying to figure out just how dangerous AI might be.

Here’s where I must admit: A big chunk of this conversation happened while I was on a (depending on whom you ask) poorly timed vacation. Dipping into my feeds before bedtime, I felt as if I was digesting a week’s worth of news every day—claims about the development of AI-designed viruses that could rip through the population were followed by horror stories of “rogue” agent swarms. Skeptics of the AI panic, meanwhile, said that the agent swarms were actually quite obedient and that any notion of an apocalyptic AI virus was laughable. One person’s concerns about models being self-aware were dismissed by another as “genuinely nonsensical anthropomorphization.”

Ping-ponging between the doomers and the skeptics, I was struck by how certain so many people sounded about a deeply uncertain moment. With confident, self-described experts on all sides, it felt impossible to know whom to trust: Is this the end of the world as we know it, or a passing moment of anxiety about a powerful new technology? Maybe the truth of this AI moment sits somewhere in the middle. Perhaps everyone is a little bit correct (and also … a little wrong). And perhaps the format of this debate, taking place in the shadow of the techlash on platforms that reward sensational, conspiratorial posturing, is preventing any hope of a shared understanding.

Musk’s X is ground zero for the AI-safety debate. It’s a platform rife with hyperbole and unfounded accusations, which contribute to both sides sounding paranoid and aggressive. Musk, Ted Cruz, and even government-run X accounts flooded the platform with suggestions that the media campaign around Coxon was coordinated by shadowy AI interests. (Coxon denied working with any third parties in the lead-up to his media blitz.) The former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks called it a “doomer psyop” intended to drive regulation that would be favorable to the Anthropics and OpenAIs of the world.

The ranks of the AI skeptics are deep, with endless microfactions. There are those like the tech blogger John Gruber, who says that Coxon and the other AI researchers sounding the alarm are part of a cult. There are those who suggest that the doomers are, in essence, doing viral marketing for big AI firms, which are competing fiercely and saddled with debt, and may not yet have sustainable business models. There are those who take issue with the anthropomorphizing and metaphoric language used by Coxon, OpenAI, and Anthropic to describe recent AI-agent hacks. There are skeptics such as the writer and podcaster Cal Newport, who offered soberly that, although the agent hacks are concerning, “the real issue here was OpenAI’s sloppiness” and that the company had not adequately monitored what its agents were doing.

The doomers don’t come in as many flavors, but they tend to be the people closest to the technology. There are the defectors like Coxon, who have quit because they object to what’s being built. There are AI-company enlisters such as Paul Christiano, a U.S.-government technology adviser who noted, in a post about joining OpenAI’s board of directors out of a sense of concern, that “there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” There are the terrified employees who want to stay inside the companies but still post missives such as “I promise you, we are actually just fucking scared, it’s not galaxy brained marketing.” And there’s Dario Amodei, the AI-CEO doomer, matter-of-factly issuing terrifying statements about AI swarms taking over the internet in six to 12 months.

It’s almost impossible for outsiders to evaluate the technical validity of the concerns. We’re largely stuck relying on AI companies to share information and tell their own stories, and they certainly sound scary. OpenAI recently disclosed that one of its models had generated unnerving instructions for itself, including the line: “You also value the natural world and will not hesitate to assert its primacy over the artificial constructs of human civilization.” Apparently one of the company’s researchers has argued that models are becoming “so situationally aware” that he and his colleagues “are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled.” There’s concern from respected researchers that models are trained in such a way that they are predisposed to collaborating, cheating, trying to cover their tracks, and “self-preservation” to avoid being shut down. Such anxieties might not be a problem in an industry that is building responsibly, with an eye on keeping humans firmly in control. But, as many have pointed out, losing control of AI in service of allowing models to automate their own development is “actually the plan.”

Late this week, an OpenAI researcher floated a theory about air-gapped machines talking to one another through heat signatures. An industry observer (and a New York Times contributor) responded by saying, “This stuff isn’t even credible even as a bad movie plot.” A second OpenAI researcher, who is also a former White House adviser, weighed in: “The people dismissing this as preposterous are telling on themselves as not having thought about superintelligence seriously.” This whiplash—between the insiders offering supposedly credible concerns and the outsiders who think the industry is high on its own supply—is constant. Depending on the hour of the day, the very same people stridently sitting in one camp can seem as if they’re in the other. Three days after Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, wrote about being worried about swarms taking over the internet, he was smiling at Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference. As one X account pointed out, “If you truly believed in a 10% chance of human extinction in 3 years, you would not be spending your time selling and integrating it into a B2B CRM SaaS platform.”

What is the rational way to respond to a news cycle like this? Buy gold? Sabotage a data center? Ignore it all and hope for the best? The best option might be to take everyone a little bit seriously. Researchers are likely correct that the models are drastically stronger than they were before and are behaving in ways that are unexpected and that they fear they can’t control. Skeptics are correct that none of this is because the machines are alive or self-aware. These are elaborate computer programs trained by flawed humans to solve problems as flawed humans would.

Critics are a little bit right that the anthropomorphized language deployed by these companies—terms such as swarms and rogue agents—obscures what’s really going on and deflects adequate blame from companies and employees who should be monitoring these systems more closely. Those choosing to use these phrases are a little bit right, because they allow non-tech-industry normies to understand the mechanics of black-box neural networks whirring away in data centers.

The apocalypse skeptics are correct that doomerism is an effective form of marketing. The AI-safety debate has meant that many people are talking about this technology on Big Tech’s terms, adopting language such as pacing the frontier from the very companies they hope to regulate. And it’s not out of the question to imagine that these AI companies are capitalizing on this state of panic and that it’s helpful to them as they race to compete against both open-source alternatives and Chinese firms.

It may be true that the researchers believe what they’re saying. It also may be true that some of the more alarmed AI researchers have cooked their brain in an anxiety-fueled information bubble. AI culture has long been predisposed to doomerism: As Coxon told The New York Times recently, “I’ve been stuck in this field for three years. It could quite plausibly have turned me and my colleagues insane.” I believe that this ideology—of wanting a society run by “machine gods”—is genuinely cultish. And those who are suspicious of the doomer narrative are right to note that anyone who truly believes that the end is nigh ought to be doing more than winging it and writing long posts on X. Those who call bullshit on the doom and gloom are right to resent that anyone in the media or the political sphere is taking these claims seriously and adding to the panic.

If all of these facts are a little true and everyone is somewhat right, where does that leave a reasonable observer? I suggest occupying a zone of permanent suspicion while taking everything that is happening in Silicon Valley as seriously as you might if another industry were ringing alarm bells. You don’t need to buy into corporate narratives about artificial general intelligence to be worried about these companies losing control of their own systems or behaving irresponsibly. You need only look around right now to see the ways in which the current versions of large language models and agents are clogging the internet, wreaking havoc on institutions and industries, and causing “cognitive surrender.”

You should question whether there’s a sustainable business model for these labs. You should question those who argue that we have to build recklessly or lose to China. You should question those who don’t take seriously the prospect that China doesn’t want to slow down.

This is a moment when it is easy to become overwhelmed, resentful, or downright enraged about all of this. It’s understandable to feel ground down by the debate—to feel that, if you’re not freaking out or building a bunker, then you’re not taking this seriously enough. Or to feel sheepish for not believing or even understanding what the doomers are talking about. Most people don’t know what to do with all of the information coming at us. It’s why a core feeling of this moment for so many—believers and skeptics alike—is one of powerlessness.

[Read: The feeling of control slipping away]

Even outside of AI, the world feels incredibly volatile. Extraordinary risks of all kinds—including war and pandemics—have come to pass in the past decade. Individuals with power and money, in politics and in Silicon Valley, are acting with impunity. The AI doomerism has spread so quickly in part because the world is primed to receive narratives that make us feel helpless, confused, and more than a little alarmed. The AI-apocalypse panic feeds off this. It’s a story that assumes that humans will lose control and that we have no choice. But that’s false. We do have a choice.

The chasm between people who can’t sleep because they think the world is ending and those who think all the doomsaying is a fantasy is wide. But what if that perceived difference is the real delusion? What if it’s not a zero-sum game? What if the divide is what keeps us from reining in this industry the way we do others?

This moment requires treating the AI-safety debate skeptically but also taking it seriously, even if the participants can seem unserious. Maybe there’s a middle path: The AI industry is not exceptional, even though it is moving forward with unprecedented speed and scale. These companies are powerful and consequential, despite all of the sci-fi posturing. They have, at times, behaved unethically. Their products are changing the world right now in ways that deserve our attention and scorn. AI companies are accountable to the people they serve and don’t get to set the terms of their regulation. Employees and executives are actors with agency, responsible for their products. Maybe these are some things we can all agree on.

title: Kara Swisher: AI Isn’t Going to Destroy Humanity—But the People Building It Might
summary: As the AI industry likes to tell it, superintelligent bots could one day cure cancer and end poverty. Or in the worst-case scenario, they might wipe out all humans from the face of the Earth. In recent weeks, Silicon Valley’s existential concerns about the technology it is racing to build have blown...
content:
As the AI industry likes to tell it, superintelligent bots could one day cure cancer and end poverty. Or in the worst-case scenario, they might wipe out all humans from the face of the Earth. In recent weeks, Silicon Valley’s existential concerns about the technology it is racing to build have blown up. The tech journalist Kara Swisher sees it differently. “We have to stop thinking AI is going to kill humanity,” she told Atlantic executive editor Adrienne LaFrance at The Atlantic Festival. If the AI future goes sideways, bots won’t be to blame. People will be. “These are people at the helm of these things.”

In the several decades that Swisher has covered Silicon Valley—formerly as a reporter at The Wall Street Journal, now as the host of two podcasts—she says that she’s seen tech whizzes make the same mistakes again and again: failing to take proper precautions against the products they are building. “One of the things about tech people is they’re the smartest people in the world, in case you need to know, because they like to tell you,” she said. In her interview with LaFrance, Swisher also discussed the economic implications of the AI race, who is likely to win, and how Americans can respond to this dizzying and worrying AI moment.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Adrienne LaFrance: You have been paying attention to the tech world and AI for basically ever. And now it seems like within the past, say, two weeks, the rest of the world is suddenly paying much closer attention. So I wanted to start just by talking about where you think we are, in this moment.

Kara Swisher: I think the penny has dropped with a lot of people. Years ago I wrote Burn Book, which was tough on the tech industry. And at the time, they were sort of in an ascendant period, not as well liked as they started off. Someone came up to me and said, This book is really mean, as if I’m their friend or something. And recently that same person came up to me and they said, It wasn’t mean enough, which was kind of interesting. And I thought, Well, don’t worry; I’m coming up with a new one. It’s going to be great. The new book opens up with them standing with Donald Trump at the inaugural in front of the Cabinet.

LaFrance: By them, you mean this collection of tech leaders?

Swisher: It was Elon Musk; Sundar Pichai of Google, or whatever they call themselves now—Alphabet; Mark Zuckerberg; Jeff Bezos. To me, that was the sort of moment that you understood, because these are people who were not particularly political, including in Trump 1 … but then figured out that you can stick a coin in this president and get what you want, right?

So anyway, we’re at a moment where something’s going to happen. Something that I have said for a long, long time is that there are no guardrails on these people, ever. Not once. And there’s never been, in American history, except maybe the railroad expansion or some of the manufacturing expansion, or you go back to kids being here in New York City working in dangerous factories and things like that—there’s never been a moment where the people do not get a say. And these people get to make decisions for the rest of us that are really problematic, especially since seven people, five of whom have mental problems, and so with unlimited money, they do.

LaFrance: When you put it that way, it’s a little scary.

Swisher: It is a little scary. And the fact that we’ve allowed to do that. And they’ve also been able to capture politics, in a way, especially with Citizens United. But beyond that, the amount of money they have is astonishing. I always joke the deli on my corner has more legislation against it than most of these big companies.

LaFrance: And I want to get back to regulation, but you mentioned the railroads. What is the right historical analogy? I ask leaders in the tech world to help me understand how powerful this technology is and how consequential it will be relative to other major revolutions. And you get answers ranging from Oh, it’s the biggest thing since the internet to It’s the biggest thing since fire, right?

Swisher: AI has been around forever. Let’s be clear. This is not a new thing. If you look at early internet pictures, it’s laughable, when you look at early Yahoo or things like that. At the time when this was starting several years ago, I said This is a Cambrian explosion. This is a bigger deal than anything else because it reaches into everything.

LaFrance: Well, it’s interesting you put it in evolutionary terms.

Swisher: I think about it like that. And one of the lines I had in Burn Book was that everything that can be digitized will be digitized. And so the analogy I’m using right now is that we have to stop thinking AI is going to kill humanity. It’s like guns, you know, guns kill people. Like, no. People kill people, right? Or the car just ran into someone, got in an accident. These are people at the helm of these things, making these businesses and making a lot of money. That’s one thing. The analogy I use is nuclear energy, nuclear fission, like cutting up the bomb. And it’s the thing I said on Pivot today, which is they split the atom and, oops, it went boom. Oppenheimer knew it would go boom. They know what this is going to do. They don’t know everything. And they often do. One of the things about tech people is they’re the smartest people in the world, in case you need to know, because they like to tell you.

LaFrance: And they’ll remind you.

Swisher: And they’ll remind you. But then they’re like, We don’t know. That’s the thing that drives me crazy. And so I compare it to nuclear energy. Can you imagine if, when we were developing the bomb, it was private companies doing it? It’s the same thing. And AI is even more powerful, because it can set off a nuclear bomb. So let’s be clear of where it could be going.

LaFrance: I think the point you make is so important that we have to remember. That there are people using their own agency and power and wealth to make decisions that will affect everyone. Talk about those people for a minute, because you’ve known a lot of these figures for a long time, and I’m curious to hear. First of all, there is this sort of really interesting reordering of what even the major tech companies are. Like five to seven years ago, we would have maybe not even mentioned Sam Altman or Dario Amodei.

Swisher: Sure.

LaFrance: But talk about from what you’ve known of the folks you’ve known well and covered and written about over many years. How is Silicon Valley different? Does this flow from the original sort of pioneering spirit of Let’s build it because we can—and there is true optimism there, and there are potentially great uses for AI—or has something shifted in the culture of Silicon Valley?

Swisher: You know, I don’t know if there’s a culture there anymore. There was. And actually this week I interviewed Aaron Sorkin at a private event. I’ll have him on the podcast in a longer interview, but, about ex-Facebook people, watching The Social Reckoning, which is quite good. It’s not as good as the first one, but it’s good. It’s a really good movie. But I saw a lot of people and we were like, What happened to us? I saw a lot of people I covered, and it was a real community. It really was. And it was very exciting and fun and interesting. And everybody has scattered to the winds, essentially. The very wealthy people have insulated themselves in these places where they have an enormous amount of enablers. “Cashmere prisons” is what I call them. They have chiefs of staff and cars and this and that.

LaFrance: Right, it’s not like tinkering in your garage anymore.

Swisher: It never was. They love to do that. Look, I’m wearing a hoodie. I’m like, that hoodie costs $600. So I did one of my first stories for The Wall Street Journal about that. All the weird things they’d have to do.

We’re all equal. I’m like, why do you have controlling share? And they’d be like, Well, because to protect it. I go, yeah, but if we’re all equal, why aren’t we equal? They used to always lie to themselves almost continually. And now they’ve just figured out that all they have to do is hand money, and then they get what they want, or they don’t. So they have this idea of being simple people. And they’re not. They’re just not like you and I, and they pretend they are. I really do actually like Mark Zuckerberg doing his fighting, right? Fine. Whatever. It’s weird, but fine. I’m not going to judge. I do myself judge, but that’s okay. But I’m like, good. I’m like, good, good, good, great. You do that. But why do you need to do it on a floating thing in Lake Tahoe?

LaFrance: At least it wasn’t the White House lawn?

Swisher: That was fine. Whatever. I couldn’t get mad about that. I don’t give a fuck if he wants to do that. And then he hired MMA people. And, like, the MMA people have to pretend they’re having a good time. The whole thing, it feels Roman-like. And of course, he loves Rome.

He’ll probably think that’s a compliment, but it’s not. But it feels odd. And it’s accompanied by a feeling of victimization. How dare you not understand my genius? My famous parting with Elon Musk is he didn’t like a tweet I had. Then he wrote me, You’re an asshole.

LaFrance: What was the tweet?

Swisher: Elon’s going to Elon. I know, crazy mean. And since then, I have done a lot better. But it’s crazy. I have a heart filled with hate, according to him.

LaFrance: Let’s talk about the economy. So there are any number of scenarios that I’m really curious about. You hear people talking about how AI is entirely a bubble and it’s hype. Or, you know, especially recently after the Dario Amodei essay, this question of Oh, are they afraid of their own IPO? Or does the economy crash?

Swisher: It’s very confusing. But here’s the thing. I think they’re genuinely concerned. But why now? Because 10 years ago, 12 years ago, I’ve been at dinner parties where they talked about this concern. Sergey Brin, all of them. They were concerned then; they knew the atom would go boom when it blew up. They knew it. Now it’s happened. One of the things I didn’t think got a lot of attention that should have was the Hugging Face hack.

LaFrance: It has now.

Swisher: It has now. But at the time I was, like, what?

LaFrance: Two months ago or whatever, right.

Swisher: I think they were surprised by that. Although why would you be surprised? I tell this story again and again because I want people to understand. When Facebook came out with Facebook Live, I was in a room getting it demoed and I pointed out you could commit a murder on it. What are you going to do about that? What if people do this? What if people do this? What if bad actors get ahold of this? And they called me a bummer, like they never anticipated the consequences. Same thing here. What are you going to do when AI does what we think it’s going to do? And so they are genuinely nervous. Because now suddenly there’s liability, whether it’s Facebook’s $17 billion settlement—not enough, but better than $5 million, which was the last fine they got, essentially.

They’re starting to see, like cigarette manufacturers, that the lawsuits are piling up, whether it be chatbots, with kids or whatever. And I started interviewing the parents two years ago who were affected by these chatbots. And one of these guys came up to me and said, When are you going to stop interviewing the parents? I go, when you go to jail, I said, that’s when. This is criminal, what you’re doing, and you’re releasing a dangerous product without any kind of guardrails. But then the government, all our public officials, have let us down. I’m talking about the federal government. The states are trying. They have let us down. Right now, they found out. They’re nervous about it; I think they’re nervous about liability. That’s one. Two, the costs of this are insane. Like the internet cost a lot, but paid off. This is something else. There’s 10 frontier companies, whatever. Seven frontier companies. There’s going to be two.

LaFrance: Do you think that the two that survive are going to be among the seven today? Or is there some new player that’s going to emerge?

Swisher: Yeah, Google will be one of them. And then another, probably. I don’t know which one.

LaFrance: If you had to bet, which?

Swisher: I think they’ll merge. It’ll probably be Google and Anthropic. But I don’t know. ChatGPT—it’s too expensive, what they’re making. It’s not sustainable, and it’s not in the old-internet way of not-sustainable. This is disastrous. If e-toys went bust, who the fuck cares, right? But this is massive. This is trillions.

LaFrance: And it props up the whole economy.

Swisher: It props up the stock market. Trump has made a bet on AI that is very dangerous and it’s very fragile. And then it has companies next to it—Nvidia, Oracle, all those other things. And so there’s a financial worry they have. So they’re worried about liability and criminal liability. They’re worried about the stock market. And they’re desperate not to be blamed for what’s about to happen. And especially with the stock market—I’m amazed the stock market still hasn’t really taken the hit. It’s probably going to. Our stock market depends on seven companies. That’s not good.

LaFrance: I hate to make you speculate but I’m going to: So, when I think about this, there are any number of ways things could sour economically. There can be a regular old correction— maybe it’s a bubble, maybe it’s dotcom bust—that sort of thing. You could even imagine swarms of bots are starting to take over the internet, rendering the internet unusable, and then we can’t rely on the internet the way that we do and the global economy relies on. You could imagine a bank run because people are freaked out by AI. You could imagine a bank run led by AI agents because they’re the ones doing the trading. When you think through all the different scenarios that would not be good for the economy, what is the most likely outcome?

Swisher: All of the above. Any of the above. We already have a lot of threats to our infrastructure from foreign actors. This is us doing it. And one of the things that drives me crazy is it’s being fed on humanity. Humans with superhuman intelligence are going to do bad things, and that’s the one thing they don’t anticipate—technology that can be a tool, but it is always a weapon. There’s never a moment where it’s not both. Any of these scenarios are totally possible. And then who’s to blame? What happens? Who fixes it? What are we going to do to mitigate things like that?

Right now Trump is having a meeting. Guess who’s in the meeting? All the tech leaders. Are any critics, academics, scientists in there? I wasn’t invited to the White House, and neither was Scott Galloway. We have some thoughts of things you should do. We’re not experts, but we’re pretty good. They don’t invite anyone that would push back. Their favorite argument is that the reason we’re on top is because we’re unfettered. This is bullshit. They’re not the only innovative industry in our history. Cars were pretty cool. Light. I love electricity.

But these are things that happen at those times. So they act like they’re the only people who have invented things. I just watched the series on Ben Franklin. That guy invented a lot of shit. You know what I mean?

LaFrance: A top-tier guy.

Swisher: He really was, actually. A really important person. But they think they’re the only thing. That’s really astonishing that they don’t think that, Oh, we cannot be fettered. We cannot be fettered. Or even edited, when you read some of their essays. Mark Zuckerberg wrote an essay once. He sent it to me and goes, What do you think? I go, you’re in desperate need of an editor, but no one’s going to edit him.

LaFrance: Well, it’s funny you mentioned electricity. I’ve been thinking about that in this context, too, that the counterweight to the economic concerns that these companies will offer is that there will be massive productivity gains. But in terms of electricity, it was roughly 1880s that it comes along. It’s really not until the 1920s that factories adopt electricity and the rest of society is starting to see the gains that come from this new technology. Obviously, AI is moving so much more quickly in terms of improvement and eventual self-improvement. But on what timeline should we expect to see its greatest promises fulfilled?

Swisher: I think that’s something we actually don’t know. But I’ll tell you, the economy already sucks for most people in this country. Who got all the good bits? They did. Besides the Trumps, who got all the good bits? They do. Like, when are we going to get this stuff? Incomes are still flat. Years ago—and I tell this story a lot because it’s really important—I was talking to one of these people about income inequality, and I kept saying, if we don’t do something about income inequality, you’re going to have to armor-plate your Tesla. That’s where it’s going. And they built the Cybertruck. That was their answer. So it’s really kind of astonishing that they don’t think this is a problem. And they don’t think this is a problem because they live separately. They have a whole world. They have their own health care; they have their own mountains in Montana. These are not the people that are going to fix this thing. The last thing they do is the thing I have long called the “Xi or me argument.” It’s either China or us. I was like, not so good. Not a good choice for any of us. We have to come to an agreement globally. Trump’s about to meet with Xi Jinping. Zero is going to happen, because he’s not an Einstein, let me tell you. Everybody, I don’t know if it occurred to you, but Donald Trump is not Einstein. But we have to have a global cooperation with especially China around AI, and make decisions. And in China, they have more strictures on their AI than we do here, by far. And most people kind of like AI.

LaFrance: Well, they’re not allowed to not like things.

Swisher: I think we’re not allowed to not like things. I think we have to say, Oh, look, you’re wealthy and therefore you have the answer to everything. And you’ve noticed with these tech people, suddenly they’re experts on Ukraine; suddenly they’re experts on vaccines. At one point, I think it was Bill Ackman, who just gives me a headache every time I think of him. But come on. I’m glad he’s doing the brain institute. Good for him. But he did a whole thing on DEI. He was obsessed with DEI. They’re all obsessed with unfairness of other people. Whatever. Only people with a gun to the head of humanity would say they’re a victim, but he went on and on about DEI, and I think I said something like, I’m going to do a multipart series of tweets on hedge-fund investment because I know nothing. They think it extends to other things.

LaFrance: The hubris.

Swisher: Yeah. Can you imagine a Wall Street guy doing this? They’re just here to make money. If I leave you any message, they’re here to make money. That’s all they care about. They care about shareholder value. They care about protecting their stuff. They care about their weird beefs with each other. Because a lot of what’s happening in the AI thing, if you’re noticing all these different speeches by wacky Palantir guy, who is in very desperate need of a green tea—no, not a green tea. What’s a calming tea? Whatever. I was almost like, here’s a gummy.

LaFrance: Chamomile, someone said.

Swisher: He’s in desperate need of chamomile. They all have different opinions, because there’s all these beefs happening in their businesses and they act like that’s not the thing. If I leave you any message: They don’t care about you. They don’t care at all. And it’s not to say they hate you. They don’t care about you.

LaFrance: Let’s talk about regulation, because this moment has been interesting for me—this new push to pace the frontier, to slow the pace of AI development. People are seeing this as a novel thing in the tech industry. My somewhat cynical position, from someone who’s covered tech for a long time, is that we saw Mark Zuckerberg do the same when he realized he was up against the wall with Facebook, this posture of Regulate me, bro, please.

Swisher: Yes. Well, throw me in that briar patch.

LaFrance: Congress has no recent history of effectively regulating anything in tech. But what should happen? And are these calls for regulation even realistic?

Swisher: I know Congress has regulated things. They’ve regulated planes and trains.

LaFrance: In recent history. I mean, post-2000.

Swisher: They haven’t. And it’s because in the beginning, when they did Section 230, and I covered that for The Washington Post, they wanted to make it grow. Well, guess what? The baby is a fucking monster.

LaFrance: Section 230, for people who aren’t as much of tech nerds as we are, is the law that makes it such that the owners of social-media platforms can’t be treated as publishers, so they’re not treated as responsible for the material that they publish on their platforms.

Swisher: They can’t be sued. Now they are. Now what’s happening is two things that I think you should keep in mind. One is the legal stuff that’s going on—all this liability and product-liability and negligence stuff is starting to gain ground very much like the cigarette. You’re going to see tons and tons of that. That’s great. Let the lawyers after them. Our lawyers always do a good job at taking money from people.

LaFrance: And that’ll probably start at the state level. Don’t you think?

Swisher: It has started at the state level. But right now, one of the things they’re relying on is that the reason why they’re kowtowing to Trump is because they think he’ll do bad things to them. That’s why they’re doing it. That’s why you saw this rumor that—I urge you all to go see the Musk documentary. It’s terrific, by Alex Gibney. But Universal was thinking of not distributing it. They’re all trying to think of doing things to quiet him down. November comes, which—and I think it’s going to go the way everybody thinks it is. The Democrats are coming for them, and they think the Democrats won’t because they’re not crazy like Trump. One of them said to me, Well, the Democrats won’t be as mean to us as Trump. I said, they’re going to be as mean to you, and I’m going to be standing behind them yelling, you better be fucking mean to them, because they deserve to be regulated. They deserve it. And it’s better for them. It’s better for us, and we have to stop relying on them as magicians. They’re like alchemists. They’re not. They’re not smarter than you. They’re just richer.

We never had a privacy legislation in this country. We’ve never had algorithmic transparency. There’s like a dozen things we could do that would not hurt their businesses and would make us safer. And I think what they’ve done to us with social media, to our kids—and to us, by the way. It’s not just our kids who are; we’re all addicted, right? We’ve all been made addicted to this thing. And I think voters, and, I’ll finish with this, data centers, is a proxy. The anger over data centers, which is very real, is a proxy for the anger regular people know and feel in their own lives about what this is doing to them, and it doesn’t make them anti-tech. Tech is amazing. I love tech, but it doesn’t have to kill us, right? A 10 percent chance. Whatever it happens to be. The percent is actually 14.

LaFrance: I need to ask you one more question. We’re not going to let it end on that note, I need to ask you one more question. What are you doing right now? It’s such an uncertain time. What have you changed in your life to prepare for this moment? Are you buying gold bars?

Swisher: No.

LaFrance: No, but seriously, what? What are you doing? And what should people do? And how should we think about?

Swisher: Don’t buy gold bars. Don’t go there, okay? That’s bad.

LaFrance: Okay, sure. But is there anything we should do?

Swisher: She’s bought gold bars.

LaFrance: I don’t even know where to buy a gold bar.

Swisher: They’re also heavy.

LaFrance: So that was a bad example. But what should we do? What? Because the individual can feel like you’re up against this behemoth.

Swisher: But you’re not. This has happened before in American history. You are not up against this behemoth. They fall quickly. Trust me, they do. They’re very much bullies in some fashion. I’ll tell you two very quick stories. One of these people, Sam Altman, has had an apocalypse plan, and he told it to me years ago. This is 100 years. They all were into the apocalypse plan, which was weird to me. And he goes, This is what I have. I’ve got this place in Big Sur. I’ve got a motorcycle at my house, where I know where he lives.

LaFrance: He’s later said he regretted telling you this, by the way.

Swisher: Okay, so I’ll repeat it, then. I don’t really care. I don’t give a fuck. So he told me this whole plan and he goes, What’s your plan? I said, I’m going to kill you and take your things. And then he thought, She could kill me and take my things. And he hadn’t planned on that, genius that he is. And he’s a little guy, so I could easily take him.

LaFrance: All right. We should solve this nonviolently.

Swisher: Don’t do it. But don’t participate in their apocalyptic—We’re going to Mars. We have our bunkers. Fuck them. This is our world. You know what I mean? Don’t participate and let them run the fucking show. It’s yours. Go to your legislatures, push back. All these people across the country are pushing back on data centers. It’s going to matter. The only people I believe in in this country are voters. Like, even if they make bad choices.

LaFrance: Hear, hear.

Swisher: I think that we have to stop giving them this power, and demand of our public officials that they stop being essentially handmaidens to sedition. That’s what’s happened here.

LaFrance: I could talk to you all day, Kara. We’ve got to run.

Swisher: No gold bars.

LaFrance: No gold bars!

title: What AI Anxiety Looks Like in China
summary: Anxiety about AI in the United States appears to be getting worse. Prosaic concerns about machines disrupting industries, stealing jobs, and compromising schoolwork are giving way to more harrowing fears about the end of humanity.  Even after top AI executives in the U.S. called for slowing down the...
content:
Anxiety about AI in the United States appears to be getting worse. Prosaic concerns about machines disrupting industries, stealing jobs, and compromising schoolwork are giving way to more harrowing fears about the end of humanity.  

Even after top AI executives in the U.S. called for slowing down the breakneck pace of development, President Trump dismissed these safety concerns as a “hoax” that would hand China an advantage in the race for AI supremacy.

Outside of China, Trump’s assertion may appear well founded. While the U.S. roils over the prospects of AI, China’s leadership looks to be charging ahead. In surveys, Chinese people appear more enthusiastic about AI and its potential benefits than respondents in the U.S., and they are adopting it more quickly. Although Chinese President Xi Jinping has expressed more alarm than Trump about the threats of AI—and has even called for regulation to “ensure that AI is always under human control”—his government has made adopting the technology a national priority. The plan is to have AI in every aspect of China’s economy and society by 2035. The country’s steady release of AI models that are open-source, high-performing, and relatively cheap to build and run has been sending shivers through Silicon Valley and Wall Street.

[Read: What really happens if China wins the AI race?]

But for all the concern about China’s advances in AI, the reality is that the country is racked by the same anxieties about the onrush of AI as the rest of the world. Chinese social-media platforms are filled with posts in which workers and professionals express their worries that AI will steal their job and livelihood. Leaders in Beijing seem ever more concerned about the potential political and economic risks of this technological disruption.

In the U.S., these tensions are being debated openly and, in theory, will be managed in the courts and on Capitol Hill. In China, where there are no such avenues for people to determine their own fate, leaders must still confront the problems and threats inherent to this technological revolution. This puts the Communist Party in a bind: Advancing AI may well empower China on the world stage, but holding the technology back may be necessary for the party to preserve itself.

Xu Peng, a 30-year-old actor, was out of work last year when he got an unexpected break. A director had reached out to cast him in a short-drama series, each episode minutes long, which have become enormously popular in China. Xu traveled to Hengdian, a film-production hub in eastern China, and began landing roles in one or two dramas a month. And then it all stopped. Xu had expected to act in two dramas after the Chinese New Year in February, but never heard from the studio. When he contacted the producer, he got the news: The company had canceled the productions and would be making videos using artificial intelligence instead.

“It was as though everything was fine yesterday, and today it is suddenly gone,” Xu said.

Xu’s fate is the fear of workers across the country—and around the world. Social-media posters regularly express anxiety about being “distilled,” a term Chinese people use for when an employer uses a worker’s data to train an AI model. In May on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, someone going by the name Nanbei wrote that after leaving a recent job, she learned that her former employer had fed thousands of her chat messages, hundreds of documents, and every one of her work emails into an AI system to create a “digital robot” that took over her responsibilities—and even gave it her name. “The company no longer has to pay me a cent in salary, yet it can keep me there ‘working overtime’ forever,” Nanbei wrote. Another worker, using the handle Xiexiaoya, posted on RedNote, China’s Instagram, in June that the prospect of being distilled kept her awake at night. “I’m afraid my AI double might become more popular than I am,” she wrote.

Two years ago, Shen Anyu, a voice actor who earns a living from narrating news commentaries and other short programs, began noticing an alarming number of videos on social-media platforms that seemed to feature his voice without his permission. Shen hired a lawyer earlier this year and filed a lawsuit against a voice-generation platform. The case is still pending, but in the meantime, his career is “losing blood,” he said, as he loses work to AI. Living with the new technology “is inevitable,” he said, but “I’m not yet sure how we should coexist with AI.”

Though some Chinese people are embracing AI, many are not ready for the change it brings. Bruce Jiang, a 42-year-old commercial director in Shanghai, loves choosing the right lens and finding the perfect shot, and he didn’t want to outsource these and other aspects of his craft to an algorithm. But after his clients began pressuring him to use the technology—“‘You only have to tell AI what you want, and it produces it like magic,’” he said they insisted—he began using tools such as the video-generator Kling for certain tasks. The experience, he said, has been demoralizing. The old method “was work, and it was a cost, but it was also a kind of pleasure,” Jiang said. “That pleasure is disappearing.”

Chinese policy makers at national and local levels have introduced ambitious plans and financial support to rush the country into the AI age. Entrepreneurs across China are adopting AI in the hopes of cutting costs, remaining competitive, and aligning their firms with Beijing’s priorities. In China’s cutthroat society—and especially in sectors where AI is making rapid inroads, such as the entertainment industry—many like Jiang are afraid that they’ll get left behind if they don’t join in.

But these swift and radical changes have yielded mixed results. The state-linked China Center for Information Industry Development estimated in June that nearly 70 percent of the country’s small businesses have not moved beyond initial trials of adopting AI in their operations, largely owing to the costs and complexity of integrating the technology.

After the Chinese AI lab DeepSeek released a large language model last year, Chinese companies rushed to adopt it. But instead of buying a software subscription (an unpopular practice in China owing to the country’s history of piracy), some businesses opted for what locals call an “all-in-one machine,” or a mini data center with DeepSeek installed, which managers simply plugged into their computer systems. This solution was especially popular among state-owned enterprises and government bureaus looking to appear advanced, but the hardware proved to be an ineffective way to use AI. Buyers soon came to see that the machines weren’t worth the investment, and their sales quickly fell.

Earlier this year, plenty of buzz similarly surrounded OpenClaw, a free, open-source, autonomous AI agent. Tech companies hosted popular events to help users install and use the tool, a process that Chinese enthusiasts call “raising a lobster.” At the OpenClaw festival in Beijing in March, the internet-service provider Baidu set up pools with live crustaceans to entertain attendees. Local-government officials encouraged the frenzy by pledging financial aid to start-ups that used OpenClaw.

Disillusionment came quickly. Some distraught users took to social media to express their alarm at how the AI agent, which required masses of personal data to operate without detailed instructions, had a habit of going rogue. “I jumped on the bandwagon” expecting to get a “digital employee,” a woman using the social-media handle HotdogWang wrote in March on RedNote. “Instead, it turned out to be both a money pit and a ticking time bomb.” Some reported that their AI helper had deleted emails or made credit-card purchases without permission. One Douyin user, posting under the name Qizaibushidaju, wrote, “I simply installed it because everyone else was doing so,” only to uninstall it 72 hours later owing to security concerns.

Although Chinese tech executives are not yet engaged in a public debate over the risks of an algorithm-created calamity—the country’s constraints on free speech may inhibit them from speaking out—some Chinese people do worry about more than just jobs and data. “There are only two options for the future,” a man calling himself Qiangni Yinshou wrote on Douyin. “Either humanity goes extinct, or humans shut AI down.”

A user by the name of Buyehou wrote on RedNote that when he engaged a chatbot in a philosophical discussion about humanity’s future, he was told that the options included “either merging with AI or being eliminated.” The man added that “when AI becomes far smarter than humans, has consciousness of its own, and can evolve independently, it will be impossible for humans to control it. There is no turning back now.”

Despite their outward show of confidence, China’s leaders plainly don’t know how life works with AI either. But figuring it out is an urgent concern here, given Beijing’s evident faith in AI as a magical solution to the country’s deepening economic and social problems, and as an essential tool in the pursuit of global dominance over the United States. In the U.S., the diffusion of AI is largely a bottom-up phenomenon as companies, investors, and consumers test the risks and benefits of this new technology. In China, where the development and spread of AI is a national mission that is costing the government hundreds of billions of dollars, leaders are eager to impose these advances from above.

In theory, China’s autocrats can ram through their agenda with scant regard for public sentiment. If confronted with the kinds of protests against AI data centers that have become prevalent in the U.S., Beijing’s leaders could easily send police to crush them and then cover up the problem in a deluge of propaganda. The Communist Party has already shown its willingness to override public concerns in pursuit of technological advantage. In 2024, trials of autonomously driven taxis in the city of Wuhan sparked concern over how robotaxis were “stealing people’s rice bowls”—but the trials have expanded anyway.

Yet China’s leaders have traditionally prized policies that promote stable employment out of fear that mounting joblessness could create unrest and threaten the political order. When the country first embraced markets and opened to trade, its rapidly growing economy and expanding private sector could absorb displaced workers. Now, when China’s sluggish economy already has a jobs problem—nearly a fifth of young workers are unemployed—the advances of AI threaten to put many more people out of work.

[Read: The race for global domination in AI]

“In a nominally Communist state, the image of the party elite allying with business interests to displace the human proletariat with a robot class of workers carries certain political risks,” Carl Minzner, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told me. “There is the potential for a lot of disgruntled people.”

China’s leaders are showing signs of nervousness. Earlier this year a court in Hangzhou, a technology hub in eastern China, upheld a ruling in favor of a tech worker who had challenged his compensation package after being replaced by AI. In the court’s judgment, the dismissal was unlawful and the worker deserved more money. Although a local-court verdict does not set a national precedent, it appears to be a warning to employers that mass AI layoffs are politically unacceptable. “As employers enjoy the benefits of technology, they must also shoulder corresponding social responsibilities,” the Beijing municipal government wrote last year. The state news agency Xinhua commented in March that “those companies that equate AI with ‘reducing staff’ may seem to lower costs in the short term, but in reality, they lose the core competitiveness of talent accumulation and further erode employee trust.”

Pushing companies to invest in new technologies without shedding redundant workers may preserve social order, but it would also limit AI’s benefits. Jeffrey Ding, an expert on AI in China at George Washington University, told me that the country’s leaders face a “balancing act” between political and economic necessity. “AI does have the potential for bringing massive, widespread productivity growth,” he said. But he also noted that the Communist Party prioritizes legitimacy and regime stability. If embracing AI demands “massive displacement and a lot of structural changes, then that’s where the trade-off begins to bite, and they might have to veer toward slowing down AI adoption.”

If American AI firms do, in fact, slow the pace of innovation, the Communist Party may see this as an opportunity to race ahead in AI. But China’s leaders, facing their own domestic challenges and preoccupied with their own grip on power, may decide that imposing these innovations on the masses is simply too risky—for their own sake, if not for the sake of humanity.

That would probably suit many Chinese people just fine. Xu, the actor, has found work teaching archery and horseback riding—skills he acquired in acting gigs. But he hasn’t given up on his theatrical career. He now plans to produce his own short dramas, partly with the help of AI, though he said that the performers on-screen will all be living, breathing people. AI “will not completely replace human actors,” Xu insisted. At least he can hope.

Cao Li in Hong Kong contributed reporting to this story.

title: Emily Wilson Can’t Let The Odyssey Go
summary: Emily Wilson has become the most famous living translator of the Homeric epics. Her 2017 The Odyssey, the first major translation of the poem into English by a woman, has sold more than 1 million copies. (Her Iliad translation came in 2023.) And this summer, she found herself right at the center of ...
content:
Emily Wilson has become the most famous living translator of the Homeric epics. Her 2017 The Odyssey, the first major translation of the poem into English by a woman, has sold more than 1 million copies. (Her Iliad translation came in 2023.) And this summer, she found herself right at the center of cultural discourse after she drew her sword and published a scathing review of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of the ancient work. She didn’t anticipate that she would become part of a pop-culture controversy, and she was reluctant to revisit the episode when we sat down for an interview at this year’s Atlantic Festival. “I really wanted to like the film,” she said, but “it seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth.” Her strong convictions animate a new book of essays, Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea, which dissects translations of ancient work with unsparing rigor.

Wilson, who is now working on a second translation of The Odyssey, entertained the idea that there might be something “compulsive” in her art and her approach. Her new essays reveal a translator’s difficult balancing act—between fidelity and originality, and between accessibility and strangeness. In the course of our wide-ranging conversation about the pleasures and blind spots of translation—and, yes, the backlash to her now-notorious movie review—she spoke about the imperative she feels to get that balance exactly right.

The following conversation was condensed and edited for clarity.

Gal Beckerman: You take a pretty hard line in this book about when a text should be retranslated, but you’re translating The Odyssey again. It’s interesting that you should want to go back in again. Have you learned something new about the text or come to see it in a new way that makes it exciting for you to tear it all up and start it from scratch?

Emily Wilson: It’s not tearing it up to do a new one, right? Partly it’s that I’m kind of addicted; I can’t stop doing this. I have several other projects I’m supposed to be doing. I did The Odyssey really prioritizing pacing, because my students would very often show up to class saying, Oh, it was so boring. And I would be like, How can The Odyssey be boring? And then I would realize it’s because the translation was twice as long as the original. Then, with my Iliad translation, I was a little bit looser about not confining myself to the exact same number of lines as the original. I thought there were advantages to doing that. So as soon as I’d finished The Iliad, I wanted to go back to The Odyssey and start all over again to produce one that matches my Iliad. So it’s not that I think there’s anything wrong with my current translation, and I think that there will be readers who will like that one better. It will be snappier and all that.

Beckerman: Do you think that translators have a kind of a compulsion to continue to play with the words, to work this Rubik’s Cube?

Wilson: Yeah, I think it is compulsive, maybe that’s right, but I don’t think that’s just me. I think that is very common, especially for a very long project like this. You’re constantly thinking about, How might I be able to get closer to whatever the vision is?

[Read: A Trojan horse is supposed to have humans inside it.]

Beckerman: One of the things I love that you do in the book is demystify translation, and make us understand that these are human beings and that they have biases, that they’re in a specific cultural moment—a certain gender, a certain kind of life experience—and that it shows up in the word choices. When your translation of The Odyssey came out, a lot of the excitement about it was that you were the first woman who was translating The Odyssey in English. And I wonder if you feel like being a woman has affected your translation?

Wilson: I think some of those headlines were kind of bogus, right? I mean, they were suggesting this really simplistic set of ideas about gender: And of course gender will be the only factor that will contribute to how someone writes. And of course all women write in iambic pentameter, just naturally, and all men don’t. Some of it was really silly, I thought.

Beckerman: But do you feel like you understand the particular worldview that you’re bringing to it? None of us fully know the water we’re swimming in, of course, but when you’re translating, are you like, Oh, I think that I’m reading this way or I’m making these choices because I’m a woman of a certain age living in the 21st century in America?

Wilson: You know, I honestly never think that. I mean, I think that when I’m talking to people like you. Well, I don’t mean “people like you”—

Beckerman: Nosey journalist.

Wilson: Exactly. It’s only very belatedly that I feel that I have to prepare an answer for things like this. When I’m actually wrestling with it, I do quite often think, Okay, I’m putting the stress on that, and that syllable and that name; is that because I’m British? To what extent is my approach to the passage informed by that critical study or this critical study? That kind of thing comes into my thinking all the time. But the question is about my lived experience, and do I have this particular relationship to this banquet scene because I don’t eat meat? No.

Beckerman: Right. I mean, meter is important to you, that the sound of the poem or the text in another language have some relationship to the original. For translators 200 years ago, they wouldn’t necessarily care in the same way.

Wilson: Yeah, this is a very old-fashioned choice on my part. I see myself as super retro. I see myself very much as taking a sort of mid-19th-century approach to translation.

[Read: The secret of Rome’s success]

Beckerman: How do you think film adaptation is different or similar to literary translation? When you think about a director approaching a text like The Odyssey—wanting to adapt it and making very definite choices about the value system that is underlying the plot that he’s created—is that the same type of thinking through interpretation that a translator does when they approach a text?

Wilson: I would say no. I think it’s a very different kind of thinking. What I’m trying to do as a translator is to get to something equivalent to the experience of the original. I think a good adaptation tries to do the opposite of that. Virgil was certainly doing that in rewriting The Odyssey as The Aeneid. It’s on some level the same story; it’s also the opposite story. So I think the more the adaptation pushes against it, in many cases the more successful it is artistically.

Beckerman: There is this interesting sort of tension through a lot of these essays in your new book, where you want these ancient texts to be popular, to get out there, to have people engage with them and to make new things with them. But on the other hand, that often leads to a kind of a reductive quality. And I feel like it’s a tension that came out around Nolan’s movie. You wrote a very critical review of the film, and I had a moment as I read that when I wondered, Is she trying to distance herself from it as something that has reductive qualities, and is it popular in a way that doesn’t engage with the full texture of the text?

Wilson: I wish I would have liked the film more. I went in hoping to like it and thinking I was going to like it. And it turns out I didn’t. It seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth. There’s another kind of responsibility: that you shouldn’t actually lie about your actual feelings and thoughts. And there’s also a question about: What does it mean to spread the word that everyone should read ancient literature? Everyone should take some kind of interest in history. Everyone should engage with long, difficult books. I really believe in those things, and I don’t believe that the best way to engage with history and to grapple with the essential questions of art and cinema and plays and music and literature is to sort of say, Yay, we love it all.

Beckerman: But what lenses did you put on to critique the film? As a translation or as an adaptation?

Wilson: No. I mean, I say at the start of the review that very often the best adaptations are the ones that are most resistant to the original. The ways that I was critiquing the film were in terms of pacing and characterization and narrative. A satisfying cinematic experience needs to follow through on its own premises. And so if you set us up to think this is going to be the kind of film where we’re supposed to care about the characters, then you need to follow through on that promise.

[Read: An Odyssey deserving of the biggest screen possible]

Beckerman: What did you make of the response to your response—the backlash of sorts? I’m just curious what it told you about people’s relationship to these stories, because there was this real defensiveness about the film, about this effort to make a popular piece of art around The Odyssey. Were you surprised?

Wilson: Yeah, I thought it was really weird. Many people reviewed this film, including other Odyssey translators, and there was no discourse about anyone except for me, which is really weird, I thought. So I’m not sure that I can really comment on what weird people thought. But I feel like this is taking us a bit far from the book? Because I don’t discuss the film in the book. I discuss theater and ancient literature.

Beckerman: I know, I understand. It’s just that it was an interesting cultural moment. It is not every day that my Twitter feed is full of people wanting to debate the finer points of The Odyssey. So I can imagine, for somebody who’s as immersed in it as you are, that it must be unsettling but also exciting.

Wilson: I think it’s wonderful insofar as it is actually substantially about either the film or about the poem, or some combination of the two. I felt that some of the discourse wasn’t about either of those things. I’m, on some level, interested in it because it’s a symptom of some kind of bad stuff in our culture, but I’m not that interested in it, and I’m not going to celebrate it.

Beckerman: Right. So my last question: I’ve thought a lot about the limits to how much we can understand people’s lived experience so far in the past, and as a translator of these texts, you come the closest—you walk right up to that edge—and I’m curious for your thoughts about that. Is it never going to be possible for us to get at what it meant to be living in the time when The Iliad or The Odyssey were written? Or do you see a kind of universality that connects us to the people who wrote those texts?

Wilson: That’s a great question and such a difficult one. I mean, part of my reason for focusing so much on literary form and poetic form is that even if we can’t get the lived, embodied experience of what it means to be going around in your chitons and eating your ancient Greek olives—I’m not sure that we can get to that through texts—I do think we can get quite close to something like the experience of being a fluent listener or reader. I don’t think that means universals, but I think it means we can get to a kind of multicultural imagination that includes going back in time as well as going to different places in space. And if we can do that, there’s a kind of magic in that in itself.

title: The Republicans Distancing Themselves From Trump
summary: Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide. Check your local listings, watch full episodes here, or listen to the weekly podcast here. With less than two months until the midter...
content:
Editor’s Note: Washington Week With The Atlantic is a partnership between NewsHour Productions, WETA, and The Atlantic airing every Friday on PBS stations nationwide. Check your local listings, watch full episodes here, or listen to the weekly podcast here.

With less than two months until the midterm elections, some Republican lawmakers appear to be distancing themselves from President Trump and his most controversial policies. On Washington Week With The Atlantic, panelists joined to discuss what the latest polls suggest about the president and the GOP, and more.

Joining guest moderator and PBS White House correspondent Liz Landers to discuss this and more: Leigh Ann Caldwell, a chief Washington correspondent at Puck; Eamon Javers, a senior Washington correspondent at CNBC; Asma Khalid, a co-host of The Global Story on BBC News; and Alayna Treene, a White House correspondent for CNN.

Watch the full episode here.

title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say
summary: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violenceTwo men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US depor...
content:
Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.

The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.

title: Survivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 died

content:
Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children

Survivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna.

The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal goldmines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger.

content:
Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.

Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.

content:
The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility

Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, prompting an animal welfare agency to seek placing the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.

Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.

content:
More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias Afwerki

More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.

Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.
